children.translated_text: Since the accomplishment of all human aims is preceded by correct knowledge, that is here explained.
Correct knowledge is twofold.
It is perception and inference.
Among these, perception is free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous.
Conceptual construction is a cognition whose appearance is fit to be connected with verbal expression.
Knowledge devoid of that, and not affected by a distortion produced by eye disease, rapid whirling, travel in a boat, agitation, and the like, is perception.
That is of four kinds.
Sensory cognition.

children.text: svaviṣayānantaraviṣayasahakāriṇā indriyajñānena samanantarapratyayena janitaṃ tan manovijñānam ||
children.translated_text: That mental cognition is produced by sensory cognition, whose immediately preceding condition assists with respect to the object immediately following its own object.
There is self-awareness of all minds and mental factors.
And yogic cognition is born from the culmination of intensified cultivation of a real object.
Its object is the particular characteristic.

children.text: yasya arthasya saṃnidhānāsaṃnidhānābhyāṃ jñānapratibhāsabhedas tat svalakṣaṇam ||
children.translated_text: That object whose appearance in cognition differs according to its presence or absence is the particular characteristic.
That alone is ultimately real.
For a real thing is characterized by the capacity to perform an effective function.
The other is the general characteristic.
That is the object of inference.

children.text: tad eva ca pratyakṣaṃ jñānaṃ pramāṇaphalam ||
children.translated_text: And that very perceptual cognition is the result of the means of knowledge.
Because it has the nature of cognition of the object.
Its conformity to the object is the means of knowledge.
For the cognition of the object is established under the control of that.
Inference is twofold.
It is for oneself and for another.

children.text: tatra svārthaṃ trirūpāl liṅgād yad anumeye jñānaṃ tad anumānam ||
children.translated_text: Among these, inference for oneself is the knowledge concerning what is to be inferred that arises from a sign having three characteristics.
Here too the arrangement of means of knowledge and result is as in perception.

children.text: trairūpyaṃ punar liṅgasya anumeye sattvam eva sapakṣa eva sattvam asapakṣe ca asattvam eva niścitam ||
children.translated_text: The threefold character of the sign is this: its certain presence in what is to be inferred, its presence only in similar cases, and its certain absence in dissimilar cases.
Here the subject, qualified by the particular property one wishes to know, is what is to be inferred.
A similar case is an object that is similar through the general property to be proved.
A dissimilar case is what is not a similar case.

children.text: tato anyas tadviruddhas tadabhāvaś ca iti ||
children.translated_text: That is, what is other than it, what is opposed to it, and what lacks it.
And the three-charactered signs are only three.
They are non-apprehension, essential nature, and effect.

children.text: tatra anupalabdhir yathā, na pradeśaviśeṣe kvacid ghaṭaḥ upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasya anupalabdher iti ||
children.translated_text: Among these, non-apprehension is as follows: there is no pot in some particular place, because what would meet the conditions for apprehension is not apprehended.
Meeting the conditions for apprehension consists in the completeness of the other causal conditions of apprehension and in a particular nature.

children.text: yaḥ svabhāvaḥ satsv anyeṣu upalambhapratyayeṣu san pratyakṣa eva bhavati sa svabhāvaviśeṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: The particular nature is that nature which, when the other causal conditions of apprehension are present, becomes directly perceptible.
Essential nature is a reason for a property to be proved that exists merely through the existence of itself.
For example, 'This is a tree, because it is a śiṃśapā.'

children.text: kāryaṃ yathā vahnir atra dhūmād iti ||
children.translated_text: An effect is as follows: 'There is fire here, because there is smoke.'
Here two reasons prove real entities, and one is a reason for negation.

children.text: svabhāvapratibandhe hi saty artho arthaṃ gamayet ||
children.translated_text: For an object indicates another object when there is a natural connection.
Because, for something not connected with that, there is no necessity of invariable concomitance with it.

children.text: sa ca pratibandhaḥ sādhye arthe liṅgasya ||
children.translated_text: And that connection of the sign is with the object to be proved.
In reality, it is through identity with it and through origination from it.
For what is not of that nature and what is not produced from that is, with respect to it, of an unconnected nature.

children.text: te ca tādātmyatadupattī svabhāvakāryayor eva iti tābhyām eva vastusiddhiḥ ||
children.translated_text: And those two, identity and origination from it, belong only to essential nature and effect; therefore a real entity is established only by those two.
The establishment of negation, too, comes from the very non-apprehension described above.
Because, when the thing exists, that non-apprehension is impossible.

children.text: anyathā ca anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpteṣu deśakālasvabhāvaviprakṛṣṭeṣv artheṣv ātmapratyakṣanivṛtter abhāvaniścayābhāvāt ||
children.translated_text: Otherwise, since the cessation of one's own perception would not establish absence for objects remote in place, time, or nature though meeting the conditions for apprehension, there would be no certainty of absence.

children.text: amūḍhasmṛtisaṃskārasya atītasya vartamānasya ca pratipattṛpratyakṣasya nivṛttir abhāvavyavahārapravartanī ||
children.translated_text: The cessation of a cognizer's present perception, when the memory impression is not confused, is what initiates practical treatment of absence for what is past and present.
Because from that very cessation there is certainty of absence.
And according to differences of application, it is of eleven kinds.

children.text: svabhāvānupalabdhir yathā na atra dhūma upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptasya anupalabdhir iti ||
children.translated_text: Non-apprehension of the essential nature, as in: 'There is no smoke here, because what would meet the conditions for apprehension is not apprehended.'

children.text: kāryānupalabdhir yathā na iha apratibaddhasāmarthyāni dhūmakāraṇāni santi dhūmābhāvād iti ||
children.translated_text: Non-apprehension of an effect, as in: 'Here there are no unimpeded capable causes of smoke, because smoke is absent.'

children.text: vyāpakānupalabdhir yathā na atra śiṃśapā vṛkṣābhāvād iti ||
children.translated_text: Non-apprehension of the pervader, as in: 'There is no śiṃśapā here, because there is no tree.'

children.text: svabhāvaviruddhaupalabdhir yathā na atra śītasparśo vahner iti ||
children.translated_text: Apprehension of what is opposed to the essential nature, as in: 'There is no cold touch here, because there is fire.'

children.text: viruddhakāryaupalabdhir yathā na atra śītasparśo dhūmād iti ||
children.translated_text: Apprehension of an opposed effect, as in: 'There is no cold touch here, because there is smoke.'

children.text: viruddhavyāptaupalabdhir yathā na dhūmabhāvī bhūtasya api bhāvasya vināśaḥ hetvantarāpekṣaṇād iti ||
children.translated_text: Apprehension of what is pervaded by the opposed, as in: 'The destruction of an entity, even one that has come into being, is not inevitably accompanied by smoke, because it depends on another cause.'

children.text: kāryaviruddhaupalabdhir yathā na iha apratibaddhasāmarthyāni śītakāraṇāni santi vahner iti ||
children.translated_text: Apprehension of what is opposed to an effect, as in: 'Here there are no unimpeded capable causes of cold, because there is fire.'

children.text: vyāpakaviruddhaupalabdhir yathā na atra tuṣārasparśo vahner iti ||
children.translated_text: Apprehension of what is opposed to the pervader, as in: 'There is no frosty touch here, because there is fire.'

children.text: kāraṇānupalabdhir yathā na atra dhūmo vahnyabhāvād iti ||
children.translated_text: Non-apprehension of the cause, as in: 'There is no smoke here, because there is no fire.'

children.text: kāraṇaviruddhaupalabdhir yathā na asya romaharṣādiviśeṣāḥ saṃnihitadahanaviśeṣatvād iti ||
children.translated_text: Apprehension of what is opposed to the cause, as in: 'This person does not have particular signs such as horripilation, because of the presence of a particular fire nearby.'

children.text: kāraṇaviruddhakāryaupalabdhir yathā na romaharṣādiviśeṣayuktapuruṣavān ayaṃ pradeśaḥ dhūmād iti ||
children.translated_text: Apprehension of an effect of what is opposed to the cause, as in: 'This place does not contain a person marked by particular signs such as horripilation, because there is smoke.'

children.text: ime sarve kāryānupalabdhyādayo daśānupalabdhiprayogāḥ svabhāvānupalabdhau saṃgraham upayānti ||
children.translated_text: All these ten applications of non-apprehension, beginning with non-apprehension of an effect, are included within non-apprehension of the essential nature.
Even when there is a difference in formulation, in the indirect injunction or prohibition of another object.

children.text: prayogadarśanābhyāsāt svayam apy evaṃ vyavacchedapratītir bhavati iti svārthe apy anumāne asyāḥ prayoganirdeśaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Because, through repeated practice in seeing such formulations, one also comes by oneself to understand exclusion in this way, this statement of its formulation is given even for inference for oneself.

children.text: sarvatra ca asyām abhāvavyavahārasādhanyām anupalabdhau yeṣāṃ svabhāvaviruddhādīnām upalabdhyā kāraṇādīnām anupalabdhyā ca pratiṣedha uktas teṣām upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptānām ||
children.translated_text: And everywhere, in this non-apprehension that establishes practical dealings concerning absence, the things beginning with what is opposed by nature, whose negation has been stated through the apprehension of their causes and so on, and through the non-apprehension of causes and so on, are to be understood as qualified by the condition of being apprehensible.
Only their apprehension and non-apprehension are to be understood as such.
For, in other cases, opposition and the relation of effect and cause are established.
Because, even when a means of valid cognition has ceased, the nonexistence of the object is not established.
